title: "VRTs"
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
```

`freezebase.vrt` builds GDAL virtual rasters in Python and chains them into one lazy recipe.
These lines mosaic two Copernicus DEM tiles, put them onto MGRS square `32TMS25` around the
Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau, convert the heights from the EGM2008 geoid to the WGS 84
ellipsoid, and write a COG:

```{python}
import os

os.environ["PROJ_NETWORK"] = "ON"  # let PROJ fetch the geoid grid; set before rasterio loads

from pyproj import CRS
from rasterio.enums import Resampling

from freezebase import vrt
from freezebase.mgrs import MGRSGeoBox

square = MGRSGeoBox.from_mgrs("32TMS25", resolution=20.0)
names = [f"Copernicus_DSM_COG_10_N46_00_E{lon:03d}_00_DEM" for lon in (7, 8)]
tiles = [f"https://copernicus-dem-30m.s3.amazonaws.com/{n}/{n}.tif" for n in names]

dem = (
    vrt.mosaic(tiles)
    .reproject(
        src_crs="EPSG:4326+3855",  # WGS 84 with heights above the EGM2008 geoid
        crs=CRS(square.crs).to_3d().to_wkt(),  # UTM zone 32N with ellipsoidal heights
        resolution=20.0,
        bounds=square.boundingbox,
        resampling=Resampling.bilinear,
    )
    .set(band_names=["height"], units=["m"])
)
dem.to_cog("32TMS25.tif")
dem
```

Each tile is a 42 MB file, and neither was downloaded in full. GDAL read the blocks under
the square, about 4 MB, and PROJ fetched the part of the geoid grid it needed. Every height
rose by about 53 m, the distance between geoid and ellipsoid in this area. GeoTIFF has no
code for UTM with ellipsoidal heights, so GDAL keeps that CRS in `32TMS25.tif.aux.xml` next
to the COG, where GDAL-based tools such as Rasterio and QGIS find it. Keep the two files
together; on S3, freezebase reads the COG without its sidecar.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "The COG: Copernicus DEM GLO-30 on MGRS square 32TMS25 as heights above the WGS 84 ellipsoid, shaded from the northwest."
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.patheffects as pe
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.cm import ScalarMappable
from matplotlib.colors import LightSource, Normalize
from pyproj import Transformer
import rasterio

with rasterio.open("32TMS25.tif") as src:
    height = src.read(1)

left, bottom, right, top = square.boundingbox
norm = Normalize(vmin=height.min(), vmax=height.max())
shaded = LightSource(azdeg=315, altdeg=45).shade(
    height, cmap=plt.get_cmap("cividis"), norm=norm, blend_mode="soft", dx=20.0, dy=20.0
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.5))
ax.imshow(shaded, extent=(left, right, bottom, top))
fig.colorbar(
    ScalarMappable(norm=norm, cmap="cividis"), ax=ax, label="ellipsoidal height (m)", shrink=0.85
)
to_utm = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", square.crs.epsg, always_xy=True)
peaks = {"Eiger": (8.0053, 46.5775), "Mönch": (7.9967, 46.5586), "Jungfrau": (7.9631, 46.5367)}
for peak, (lon, lat) in peaks.items():
    x, y = to_utm.transform(lon, lat)
    ax.plot(x, y, marker="^", color="white", markeredgecolor="black", markersize=7)
    ax.annotate(
        peak,
        (x, y),
        xytext=(6, 4),
        textcoords="offset points",
        color="white",
        path_effects=[pe.withStroke(linewidth=2.5, foreground="black")],
    )
ax.set(title=f"MGRS {square.mgrs_code}", xlabel="easting (m)", ylabel="northing (m)")
ax.ticklabel_format(style="plain")
```

::: {.callout-note}
The height conversion needs the EGM2008 geoid grid. The first lines set `PROJ_NETWORK=ON`
before Rasterio loads, so PROJ downloads the parts of the grid it needs; set later, it has no
effect. [VRT recipes](05-vrt-recipes.qmd#convert-heights-between-vertical-datums) shows how to keep
a local copy instead.
:::

## How it works

### Nothing is read until you write

`vrt.mosaic` read the headers of the two tiles. `reproject` worked out the target grid and
the transformation from the headers and the CRSs. Neither read a pixel. `to_cog` then ran
the whole recipe through GDAL, which read the source blocks each output block needs and
wrote the COG without loading the whole raster into memory.

### What a VRT is

A [GDAL virtual raster](https://gdal.org/en/stable/drivers/raster/vrt.html) (VRT) is a small
XML document that describes a raster built from other rasters. It contains no pixels of its
own, only the source files and how to combine them. GDAL and Rasterio open a VRT like any
other raster and read the sources only when asked for pixels. This is the XML of `dem`,
shortened and unescaped:

```xml
<VRTDataset rasterXSize="500" rasterYSize="500" subClass="VRTWarpedDataset">
  <SRS>PROJCRS["WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N", ...]</SRS>
  <GeoTransform>420000.0, 20.0, 0.0, 5160000.0, 0.0, -20.0</GeoTransform>
  <GDALWarpOptions>
    <ResampleAlg>Bilinear</ResampleAlg>
    <Option name="APPLY_VERTICAL_SHIFT">YES</Option>
    <SourceDataset relativeToVRT="0">
      <VRTDataset rasterXSize="7200" rasterYSize="3600">
        <VRTRasterBand dataType="Float32" band="1">
          <SimpleSource>
            <SourceFilename>/vsicurl/https://.../Copernicus_DSM_COG_10_N46_00_E007_00_DEM.tif</SourceFilename>
            <DstRect xOff="0" yOff="0" xSize="3600" ySize="3600" />
          </SimpleSource>
          <SimpleSource>
            <SourceFilename>/vsicurl/https://.../Copernicus_DSM_COG_10_N46_00_E008_00_DEM.tif</SourceFilename>
            <DstRect xOff="3600" yOff="0" xSize="3600" ySize="3600" />
          </SimpleSource>
        </VRTRasterBand>
      </VRTDataset>
    </SourceDataset>
    <Transformer>...</Transformer>
  </GDALWarpOptions>
</VRTDataset>
```

The outer VRT is the reprojection: its grid is the MGRS square, and the warp options include
the height conversion. The mosaic is nested inside it, where `DstRect` places the two
3600 × 3600 pixel tiles side by side. `dem.to_xml()` returns the full document.

### When to write a COG

Every read of a VRT goes back to the sources and computes the result again. A VRT suits a
result you read once, or a recipe you want to inspect and edit. Write a COG when you
read the same pixels often, when the sources are remote or the chain is long, or when other
people need a plain raster.

## Compared with GDAL tools

GDAL's command-line tools and Rasterio also build VRTs, and GDAL 3.11's
`gdal raster pipeline` chains steps in one command. freezebase writes the same format, so
any GDAL program can open its `.vrt` files. It adds a Python object you can inspect and
edit between steps, without the GDAL Python bindings, and S3 credentials that come with
the paths.

| | Builds | Result | Chaining | S3 credentials | Vertical datums |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gdalbuildvrt` | mosaics, band stacks | `.vrt` file | through files | GDAL settings or environment variables | — |
| `gdalwarp -of VRT` | reprojections | `.vrt` file | through files | GDAL settings or environment variables | converts heights |
| `gdal_translate -of VRT` | band selections, subsets, rescaling | `.vrt` file | through files | GDAL settings or environment variables | — |
| Rasterio `WarpedVRT` | reprojections | open dataset, in memory | wraps another open dataset | `rasterio.Env` | through GDAL warp options you set |
| `freezebase.vrt` | mosaics, stacks, reprojections, pixel functions, band selection, clips, color ramps | Python object, written as `.vrt`, COG or other raster | in memory | taken from the sources' paths | converts heights |

## Building blocks

`mosaic`, `stack`, `reproject` and `derive` are functions that take file paths or VRTs.
`reproject`, `derive` and the other steps below are also methods of a VRT, with the VRT as
the source. The steps return a new VRT, and a VRT passed in is copied, so editing it later
does not change the result. The deprecated `create_*_vrt` and `build_vrt_mosaic` functions
each have a replacement listed in the
[changelog](https://github.com/lqgentner/freezebase/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

### Mosaic tiles

Use `vrt.mosaic` for tiles of one dataset that share a CRS, such as the Copernicus DEM
tiles. Where tiles overlap, the pixels of the later tile in the list are used.

```python
mosaic = vrt.mosaic(["a.tif", "b.tif"], band_names=["VV"])
```

The tiles need the same band count, data types and nodata values. Tiles with different
pixel sizes need `resolution`: `"finest"` takes the smallest pixel size, and a tuple
`(x, y)` sets it. `bounds` fixes the extent, which otherwise is the union of the tiles.

### Reproject onto a grid

Use `reproject` to put a raster onto another CRS or grid, such as an
[MGRS square](01-mgrs-grid.qmd):

```python
on_square = vrt.reproject("scene.tif", crs=square.crs, resolution=10.0, bounds=square.boundingbox)
```

Without `resolution`, `reproject` picks a pixel size close to the source's.
`like="other.tif"` copies the CRS, extent and pixel size of another raster. The default
resampling is `average`, which suits a coarser target. For a finer target, as at the top
of this page, pass `Resampling.bilinear` or `Resampling.cubic`. `reproject` keeps the
source's data type, so averaging `uint16` values rounds the result: pass `dtype="float32"` to keep the
fractions. When the source and target CRS both carry heights, `reproject` also converts
them, as in the example at the top.

### Stack bands

Use `vrt.stack` to combine bands from files on one grid, such as an RGB raster from three
single-band files:

```python
rgb = vrt.stack(["red.tif", "green.tif", "blue.tif"], band_names=["red", "green", "blue"])
```

`bands` picks which bands to take from each file, for example `bands=[[1], [2, 3]]`. Files
on different grids need `reproject` first.

### Derive values

Use `derive` to compute values with one of GDAL's built-in pixel functions, such as
decibels from linear backscatter or a ratio of two rasters:

```python
db = vrt.derive("sigma0.tif", vrt.PixelFunction.db())
ratio = vrt.derive(["vv.tif", "vh.tif"], vrt.PixelFunction.div())
```

`PixelFunction` covers decibels, ratios, differences, the mean, the minimum and the
maximum, among others. With one input, `derive` converts each of its bands. With several,
it computes one band from band 1 of each. The result is `float32` with NaN as nodata unless
you pass `dtype` and `nodata`, and a nodata pixel in any input gives a nodata pixel in the
output.

### Select and label bands

Use `select` to keep some bands, in any order, and `set` to change band names, color
interpretation or units, or to add tags, without touching the pixels:

```python
scene = vrt.from_raster("scene.tif")
false_color = scene.select([4, 3, 2]).set(band_names=["nir", "red", "green"])
```

### Clip a box

Use `clip_box` to cut out part of a VRT without resampling. The box edges must lie on the
pixel grid:

```python
part = dem.clip_box(422000, 5152000, 426000, 5156000)
```

### Colorize

Use `colorize` to turn one band into a red, green, blue and alpha image through a color
ramp, for a preview or a map tile. It takes color stops or a matplotlib colormap, and
nodata and NaN pixels become transparent:

```python
preview = dem.colorize([(1000, (0, 0, 255)), (4000, (255, 255, 255))])
preview = dem.colorize("viridis", vmin=1000, vmax=4000)
```

## Chaining and saving

Every step accepts a VRT, so steps chain into one recipe that nothing reads until you write
it:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  tiles[(tiles)] --> mosaic --> reproject --> derive --> cog[(COG)]
```

```python
db = (
    vrt.mosaic(["a.tif", "b.tif"])
    .reproject(crs=square.crs, resolution=10.0, bounds=square.boundingbox)
    .derive(vrt.PixelFunction.db())
)
db.to_cog("db.tif")

with db.open() as ds:  # or read it without writing a file
    data = ds.read(1)
```

The final VRT contains a copy of each earlier step, so editing an earlier VRT afterwards
does not change `db`. A chain needs GDAL 3.11 or newer.

### Write a VRT or a raster

A VRT can be saved in three ways:

- `to_vrt("x.vrt")` writes the `.vrt` file, which is small and keeps reading from the
  sources. It returns the path, which later steps accept, so a long chain can be split into
  files that other programs open.
- `to_cog("x.tif")` writes a Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF, with an optional profile such as
  `{"compress": "zstd"}`.
- `to_raster("x.png", driver="PNG")` writes any other format GDAL can create, such as a
  plain GeoTIFF or a PNG preview.

`to_cog` and `to_raster` also take band names, color interpretation, units and tags.

### Data type and nodata

A raster file has one data type and one nodata value for all its bands. If the VRT's bands
differ, pass `dtype` or `nodata` in the profile:

```python
dem.to_cog("dem.tif", {"dtype": "int16", "nodata": -9999})
```

- `nodata` replaces each band's nodata value, and pixels that held the old value get the
  new one.
- `dtype` converts every band. Fractions are rounded and values outside the new type's range
  are clipped, so a valid value can end up equal to the nodata value: 300 written as `uint8`
  with nodata 255 becomes 255 and reads as nodata.

## Inspect and edit

`vrt.read` loads a VRT file, including one written by `gdalbuildvrt`, and `vrt.from_raster`
wraps one raster file. Change what you need, then write it:

```python
v = vrt.from_raster("scene.tif")
v.bands[0].description = "VH"
v.bands[0].nodata = 0.0
v.to_vrt("scene.vrt")
```

A `VRT` has a CRS, a transform, a size and a list of bands, and `bounds`, `res`, `shape`,
`dtypes` and `nodatavals` describe it as Rasterio would. Each `Band` lists the sources it
reads from, and `VRT.sources` lists them for the whole VRT. Printing a VRT summarizes its
grid, its bands and the steps that build it, and a notebook shows the same summary as HTML,
as at the top of this page. Neither opens a source.

## VRTs on S3

An S3 source is a `UPath` built with `make_s3_upath()`, and keeps that path's credentials and
endpoint. [Accessing S3](02-accessing-s3.qmd) describes the options.

### How source paths are saved

In Python, every source path is absolute. When `VRT.to_vrt` saves a VRT, it stores a source
path relative to the VRT if both are local or both are in the same S3 bucket. Other sources
are stored as absolute GDAL paths such as `/vsis3/bucket/tile.tif` or `/vsicurl/https://...`.
`relative=False` stores every path as absolute.

`vrt.read` reverses this: relative paths are resolved against the VRT's location, and
`/vsis3/` paths become `s3://` paths. These get the storage options (credentials and
endpoint) of the VRT if it is on S3, or the ones you pass:

```python
from freezebase import vrt
from freezebase.s3 import make_s3_upath

root = make_s3_upath("s3://bucket/run", profile="research")
local = vrt.read("warped.vrt", storage_options=root.storage_options)
tiles = local.source_files(storage_options=root.storage_options)
```

`source_files()` lists every file the VRT reads in the end, including those behind nested
VRTs and behind `.vrt` files it points to. `VRT.sources` lists only the direct sources and
reads nothing. Following a `.vrt` file over HTTPS needs aiohttp, which the `s3` extra
installs.

### Credentials

`VRT.open()` opens a VRT with the credentials its sources need, whether they are local, on
S3 or public over HTTP(S). `to_cog` and `to_raster` use the same credentials. To open a
written `.vrt` file with Rasterio yourself, wrap it in `VRT.env()`:

```python
import rasterio

path = mosaic.to_vrt("mosaic.vrt")
with mosaic.env(), rasterio.open(path) as ds:
    data = ds.read(1)
```

The S3 sources of one VRT must share their credentials, and one VRT cannot mix S3 and HTTP(S)
sources. If the VRT points to other `.vrt` files with sources on S3, pass those sources'
`storage_options` to `open()` or `env()`.
